doc.title: Reading notes - phase stability of Ca3Co4O9

pages.title: Reading notes - phase stability of Ca3Co4O9

content.text: Notes from a review of layered cobalt oxides and a solid-state synthesis textbook, on the temperature up to which Ca3Co4O9 is stable.
Ca3Co4O9 is a structure of rock-salt-type layers stacked with CoO2 layers. The thermoelectric performance comes mainly from the CoO2 layers
In air, above roughly 920-930 C it decomposes into Ca3Co2O6 and CoO. Once decomposition has progressed, it is hard to reverse by cooling

Raising the sintering temperature increases density, improves grain-to-grain contact and lowers the electrical resistivity. This holds only up to the decomposition temperature; beyond it, insulating Ca3Co2O6 mixes in and the resistivity rises
Solid-state reactions proceed only where the powders touch. Grinding and remixing in between reduces the unreacted parts
The raw material calcium carbonate (CaCO3) readily absorbs moisture from the air. The weighed amount is off by the water absorbed, and the Ca to Co ratio goes wrong
is exactly the decomposition described here
may come from a composition shift caused by moisture in the raw material, not by temperature

doc.title: Reading notes - measuring the Seebeck coefficient and its errors

pages.title: Reading notes - measuring the Seebeck coefficient and its errors

content.text: Notes from an explainer article on thermoelectric measurement and the instrument manual, on how the Seebeck coefficient is measured and where the errors come from.
The Seebeck coefficient S is found by applying a small temperature difference ΔT across the sample and using the resulting voltage ΔV: S = −ΔV/ΔT
If ΔT is measured at only one point, any offset in thermocouple placement becomes error directly. It is more reliable to vary ΔT over several points and take the slope against ΔV
Poor contact between electrode and sample makes the voltage unstable. Polish the end faces of the sample so the contact is the same every time
The electrical resistivity ρ is measured by the four-probe method. Any mistake in the cross-sectional area or the distance between probes becomes error in ρ directly
The power factor PF = S²/ρ is often used to compare samples
How I handle it in my records
For every sample, I take ΔT at 4 points at room temperature (300 K) and get S from the slope
Samples are cut to 2 × 2 × 10 mm and the end faces are polished. Dimensions are measured 3 times with calipers and averaged
, I remeasured the same sample 3 times, and the scatter in S was ±2 μV/K

messages.content: When I vary the amount of Bi substitution, what conditions should I fix first?

Fix the baseline synthesis first, then keep every other variable identical while you step the Bi level.

**What to lock in**

1. **Baseline reproducibility** – Only start the Bi‑series after the original Ca₃Co₄O₉ protocol can be reproduced reliably.  [Source: "Vary Bi substitution after baseline reproduces (0‑10 %)"][Source: "Meeting notes - next direction"]  
2. **Sintering temperature** – Use the capped 920 °C setpoint (≈ 931 °C actual) and do not exceed 930 °C. [Source: "Meeting notes - next direction"]  
3. **Pressing pressure** – Keep the pressure at 100 MPa (the value that gave the best density without cracking). [Source: "Meeting notes - next direction"]  
4. **Grinding schedule** – Apply the same two‑intermediate‑grinding routine used for sample 4/6. [Source: "Sample 6 - partial replacement of Ca with Bi"]  
5. **Raw‑material lot & drying** – Use the same CaCO₃ lot (lot A) and follow the drying‑weigh‑record protocol introduced after the failure of sample 7. [Source: "Meeting notes - next direction"]  
6. **Other composition** – Keep all reagents (Co₃O₄, Bi₂O₃ amount for the chosen Bi % only) and stoichiometry unchanged apart from the Bi substitution level. [Source: "Sample 6 - partial replacement of Ca with Bi"]  
7. **Measurement setup** – Use the identical probe spacing, ΔT‑point scheme, and calibration for Seebeck and resistivity. [Source: "Sample 6 - partial replacement of Ca with Bi"]

By holding these seven conditions constant, any change you observe in Seebeck (S), resistivity (ρ), or power factor (PF) can be attributed directly to the Bi substitution level.

---

Samples 4 and 7 used the same conditions. Why did the results differ? Base it on my records so far

Sample 4 followed the baseline recipe with the **dried CaCO₃ lot B** and gave a clean Ca₃Co₄O₉ phase, 73 % relative density, S = 127 µV/K and ρ = 8.5 mΩ·cm (PF = 1.9 µW/(cm·K²))[Source: "Sample 4 - two intermediate grindings"].  
Sample 7 was processed under the *identical* temperature, pressure and grinding schedule, but the **raw‑material lot was changed**; impurities appeared and the result could not be reproduced[Source: "Study plan and log"].  

The mismatch traces back to the **moisture state of the CaCO₃ lot**. Moisture adsorbs on CaCO₃ particles, shifting the Ca/Co ratio during weighing and producing a composition that favours the formation of secondary phases (e.g., Ca₃Co₂O₆ or residual Co₃O₄) 【Source: "Moisture adsorption by CaCO₃ skews Ca/Co ratio during weighing"]**.** This explains the impurity noted in sample 7 and the higher resistivity observed when the new lot was used[Source: "Impurity in sample 7 likely stems from moisture‑induced composition shift"].  

In short, even when sintering temperature, pressure, and grinding steps are held constant, **variations in raw‑material moisture content alter the stoichiometry**, leading to phase impurities and divergent electrical/thermoelectric performance.

---

How high can I raise the sintering temperature? Think it through from samples 2 and 3 and the furnace calibration

You can’t push the furnace much above the 920 °C set‑point without running into the Ca₃Co₄O₉ → Ca₃Co₂O₆ decomposition that spikes resistivity.

* The calibrated thermocouple shows the furnace runs hotter than the displayed set‑point, and the offset grows with temperature: 920 °C → 931 °C (+11 °C) and 950 °C → 963 °C (+13 °C)[Source: "Actual furnace temperature exceeds setpoint increasingly with heat"].  
* Sample 3, which was sintered at a nominal 950 °C, stayed denser but its resistivity worsened because the actual temperature crossed the ~930 °C decomposition threshold[Source: "Sample 3 - sintering at 950 C"].  
* To stay safely below that threshold you need the **actual** temperature ≤ 930 °C. Using the measured offset curve, a set‑point of about **910 °C** would give an actual ≈ 920 °C (≈ +10 °C offset), keeping a comfortable margin[Source: "Actual furnace temperature exceeds setpoint increasingly with heat"].  

If you place the samples toward the front of the shelf, the local temperature is 5–8 °C lower than the centre[Source: "Samples placed at front of shelf experience several‑degree lower sintering temperature"][Source: "Samples placed at front of shelf experience several‑degree lower sintering temperature"]. In that case you could raise the centre set‑point by roughly that amount (≈ +5 °C) and still stay under the decomposition limit—i.e., a **915 °C–920 °C set‑point** with front‑shelf placement.

**Bottom line:**  
* **Safe ceiling (centre placement):** ~910 °C set‑point (≈ 920 °C actual).  
* **If you use the cooler front shelf:** you can push to ~915–920 °C set‑point (still ≤ 930 °C actual). Going above those values risks the insulating Ca₃Co₂O₆ phase and a rise in resistivity.
